Daniel’s analogy is most revealing where it quietly overreaches: he moves from “there exists an adversarial initial condition” to “therefore prevention may be impossible,” as if existence in a continuous model implies practical inevitability. In dynamical systems, the “dice balanced on a corner forever” is the textbook unstable equilibrium: mathematically real, but structurally fragile—an infinitesimal deviation typically exits the equilibrium manifold. That fragility matters because concurrency bugs are not usually “one special knife-edge state” but rather *robustly reachable* bad interleavings under ordinary perturbations. If Daniel’s point is that the world is continuous and therefore always admits knife-edges, that’s true but not yet relevant to whether a software design is safe; the relevant question is whether the unsafe set has *nontrivial basin of attraction* under realistic noise, scheduling jitter, and partial information.

More importantly, Daniel’s framing treats “making something atomic” as trying to force reality into a perfect bifurcation (“either A before B or B before A”). In computer science, atomicity is primarily a *specification move*: you define an operation so that, for reasoning purposes, it appears to take effect at a single instant between invocation and response—what [Herlihy & Wing call *linearizability*](https://cs.brown.edu/~mph/HerlihyW90/p463-herlihy.pdf). That doesn’t deny the underlying continuity; it sidesteps it by requiring correctness for *all* allowed interleavings at the abstraction boundary. Done well, this is closer to “prove the dice never reaches the corner under any disturbance” than “find the exact balancing point.” The blind spot is that Daniel conflates physical implementation limits with the logical goal: good concurrency control aims not to “pick the right initial condition,” but to be correct under an adversarial scheduler *within the model*.

That said, Daniel is circling a real hardware-level sting: perfect digital bifurcation is physically approximated, not guaranteed. Synchronizers and flip-flops can enter *metastability* when signals arrive near a clock edge; the circuit may hover in an analog no-man’s-land before resolving, which is essentially the “unstable equilibrium” problem reappearing inside the abstraction. Engineers don’t “eliminate” metastability so much as manage it—reduce probability, add time for resolution, and design systems to tolerate it. The upshot is a sharper answer to Daniel’s closing question: race conditions are preventable at the level of *algorithmic correctness* (define atomic operations and prove safety for all schedules), but absolute prevention at the level of *physics* is replaced by risk management and fault containment, because the discrete abstraction is implemented by analog components that can, in rare edge cases, refuse to pick a side.
